subject: 191AFB3E5AAB4E3BB80BBCC24D349113
introduction: These readings speak of the Word of God as the first gift: the master key that opens hearts, the sun under which what is hidden in the tree appears, the source of the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, a Word that took human form and that some turn towards and some refuse. Each of the nineteen quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Wisdom in Proverbs, the letter to the Hebrews, the psalms, the Qur'an on words no sea of ink could exhaust, and John's Word made flesh. Three add a side or push back: the parable of the sower on why the same word is received so differently, the Nicene Creed on what it means to call Christ the Word, and the Tao Teh King on a first principle that cannot be named.
questions: The readings call the Word the first bestowal of God and understanding its recipient. What has a word, spoken or read, unlocked in you?
The readings say that the Word appeared in human form, and that this does not mean the body of Christ. How does that compare with 'the Word was made flesh' and with the creed?
When the Word was manifested some turned towards it and some away. What does the parable of the sower suggest about why?
One reading calls drawing together and uniting 'the most exalted Word'. What would it mean to treat unity itself as what the Word says?

outside.why: In Proverbs wisdom says: the Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
The letter to the Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
The psalm says that the entrance of thy words giveth light, and giveth understanding unto the simple.
The Qur'an says that though the sea became ink for the words of the Lord, the sea would be used up before those words were exhausted.
The letter to the Hebrews begins: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets.
The Qur'an describes itself as a revelation which the True Spirit hath brought down upon thy heart, in plain Arabic speech.
John's Gospel says that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory.
Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
John's Gospel says of the Word: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
In the parable the same seed falls by the way side, on stony places, among thorns and on good ground. Is turning towards the Word or away from it a matter of the soil, and can soil be changed?
Jesus ends many of his sayings with the words: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
The Qur'an says that His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is.
Jesus says to Philip, who asks to be shown the Father: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.

The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as God of God, Light of Light, of one substance with the Father. The reading says that the Word is the perfections mirrored in Christ, not his body. Where do the mirror and the creed agree, and where do they part?
The psalm joins word and breath: by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
John's letter says that love is of God, and that God is love.
Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
The Tao Teh King begins by saying that the name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. What is the difference between a first principle that speaks and one that cannot be spoken?
